failures.title: BMW B57D30B Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Coolant System Leaks (Expansion Tank & Hoses) - 100,000+ miles
items.whatHappens: The plastic coolant expansion tank and associated routing hoses can become brittle over time due to heat cycling. This leads to slow coolant loss or, in some cases, sudden leaks under pressure. Early warning signs include a sweet smell from the engine bay or frequent low-coolant warnings on the iDrive system.
items.repairVsReplace: This is typically resolved with targeted component replacement (£300-£800). A full B57D30B engine replacement is rarely required unless severe, ignored overheating has caused secondary head gasket failure.

items.title: DPF Clogging in Urban Use - 80,000+ miles
items.whatHappens: Frequent short journeys prevent the Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) from completing active regeneration cycles. Over time, this leads to restricted exhaust flow, reduced performance, increased fuel consumption, and persistent engine management warnings.
items.repairVsReplace: Often resolved via forced regeneration or professional DPF cleaning. If the substrate is melted or heavily ash-clogged, a full DPF replacement is necessary, but this does not typically require a full engine replacement.

failures.goodYearsLine: The B57D30B is widely regarded as a highly robust modern diesel. It resolved the catastrophic rear-mounted timing chain vulnerabilities of the older N57 generation by moving the chain to the front of the engine, making it significantly more reliable for long-term ownership .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B57D30B
variants.intro: The B57D30B engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically located on a machined pad near the oil filter housing or on the front timing cover. It is also explicitly listed on your vehicle's V5C registration document under the engine details section, or it can be definitively verified via a VIN decode through a BMW specialist. The B57D30B is frequently confused with the lower-output B57D30A (typically 265 hp) or the higher-output B57D30C (typically 340 hp). While they share the same 3.0-litre inline-6 architecture, fitting the wrong revision can result in ECU mapping conflicts, incompatible turbocharger plumbing, and different DPF/EGR configurations. Always verify the exact code before purchasing a replacement unit.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B57D30B - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used B57D30B is a viable option for this engine, provided it comes with a comprehensive service history proving regular oil changes and no history of coolant system neglect. The front-mounted timing chain design makes verifying its condition far less risky than on the older N57 generation.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned B57D30B is the most balanced choice for most owners. A reputable rebuild will replace the plastic coolant expansion tank, thermostat housing, and all critical seals with updated components, directly addressing the engine's most common minor failure points while restoring factory compression.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-value G-series hosts such as the G05 X5 or G11 7 Series, where long-term ownership is planned. An upgraded rebuild should include a verified DPF/EGR system, updated cooling components, and potentially a remapped ECU to maximise longevity and efficiency.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting your B57D30B through our vetted network ensures the work is completed by BMW specialists, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty and nationwide delivery options.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For typical host vehicles like the G30 5 Series, G01 X3, and G05 X5, current market values range from £18,000 to £45,000. A reconditioned B57D30B replacement sits comfortably within this value band, making it a financially sound investment. Even for earlier G-series hosts valued around £14,000, the combination of strong retained values and the B57's inherent reliability keeps the replacement cost well within the viable threshold.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the B57D30B engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are coolant system leaks from the plastic expansion tank and associated routing hoses, alongside DPF clogging in predominantly urban use. Typical onset for coolant leaks is between 100,000 and 180,000 miles. Symptoms include unexplained coolant loss or frequent low-coolant warnings on the iDrive system. Unlike the older N57, the front-mounted timing chain is highly reliable and rarely causes catastrophic failure.

items.question: Which BMW models use the B57D30B engine?
items.answer: The B57D30B is widely fitted across BMW's G-generation lineup, primarily powering the "30d" badges. Common hosts include the 3 Series (G20/G21 330d), 5 Series (G30/G31 530d), 7 Series (G11/G12 730d), X3 (G01 xDrive30d), and X5 (G05 xDrive30d) from 2016 onwards. Always verify your specific chassis code and engine stamping before ordering a replacement unit.

A used engine inherits the exact same cooling system wear risks unless it comes with documented, recent preventative maintenance records.
